newsitem.title: USA: NYMEX chief says talks with IPE on joint trading.
newsitem.headline: NYMEX chief says talks with IPE on joint trading.

text.p: The president of the New York Mercantile Exchange (NYMEX) said Monday that he was in talks with London's International Petroleum Exchange (IPE) about a joint electronic trading system and other links between the two exchanges.
However, the NYMEX and IPE are not contemplating a full-blown merger, said NYMEX president Patrick Thompson, in an interview with Reuters.
"There are two areas we think would be of immediate interest to our two customers," he said.

"One is cross-margining so the cost of doing business is reduced...The second area is essentially joining our contracts through electronic trading systems," which initially would mean adding the IPE's Brent crude contract to the current out-of-hours ACCESS system, he said.
NYMEX sources said back in late February that the idea of cross-margining was under discussion between the two exchanges.
Thompson said Monday that he expected to make an announcement on this later in the week.
'It's all a bit premature. We have to talk much further before we can talk about done deals or anything else," he said.

"System-wise, regulatory-wise we need to look into what the implications are and whether we can support those things. I think those are things that can be ironed out but they do take a lot of that fine print that goes into such a deal."
There is an agreement in principle between the IPE and the NYMEX that cross-margining, which effectively would reduce the amount of capital traders would have to put up, made sense for their members.

Thompson said that, for example, traders who go long the NYMEX crude contract and short the IPE's Brent contract -- a common spread trade -- have to put up margin capital for both positions. But the "portfolio risk" is just on the price differential between the two.
"So, we have common interests that we both recognize," said Thompson.
On the joint electronic system, he said that adding Brent to the ACCESS system would be the first step but that would then be a platform for further developing the electronic trading system.

"It is at the working-group stage now. We know that Brent and (the NYMEX crude contract) trade as a spread in the cash market; we have a system that is existing, the ACCESS system. Obviously, over the years that system would have to be developed," he said.

As well as benefits for the two exchanges' members, Thompson agreed that the talks were also spurred by concern that, after years of rapid growth, volumes in crude and oil product futures had been trailing off in recent years.
But despite the areas of common interest, Thompson said the two exchanges wanted to remain independent.
"Both of us intend to retain our indepenedence as institutions long after this -- a merger is not even on the table," he said.
